options: some TM halts on every input and accepts exactly the strings in L
some TM accepts exactly the strings in L, possibly looping on others
explain: Recursive means decidable: there is an always-halting TM for L. RE only asks for a recogniser.

q: L is recursive if and only if…
options: both L and its complement are RE
the complement of L is RE
explain: Run recognisers for L and L̄ in parallel. One of them must accept every input, so the combined machine always halts with the right answer.

q: Which class of languages is not closed under complement?
explain: If RE languages were closed under complement, every RE language would be recursive by the key theorem. A<sub>TM</sub> shows that is false.

q: A<sub>TM</sub> = {⟨M, w⟩ : M accepts w} is…
explain: A universal TM recognises A<sub>TM</sub> by simulating M on w. But no TM can decide it (topic 25).

q: If L is RE but not recursive, then its complement is…
explain: If L̄ were RE too, then L would be recursive by the key theorem, which is a contradiction.

options: A<sub>DFA</sub> = {⟨D, w⟩ : DFA D accepts w}
A<sub>TM</sub> = {⟨M, w⟩ : TM M accepts w}
HALT = {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w}
explain: Simulating a DFA always halts, and CFG membership is decidable (for example with CYK). A<sub>TM</sub> and HALT are RE but undecidable.

q: Recursive languages are closed under union, intersection and complement.
explain: True. Run the deciders one after the other and combine their answers. For complement, swap accept and reject.

q: A language is RE exactly when…
options: some enumerator can list all its strings
explain: An enumerator runs a recogniser on all strings, alternating steps, and prints each one that is accepted. This gives a list of L.

q: Why are most languages not RE?
options: There are countably many TMs but uncountably many languages
explain: Each TM has a finite description, so there are countably many. The subsets of Σ* are uncountable, so most languages have no TM at all.
